title: Mindfulness without ethics
hookLine: critics warn that mindfulness sold for productivity can lose its Buddhist ethical roots (Purser, 2019)

lines: WHAT IF THE STRESS SHOULD CHANGE?
cards: A calendar invite lands in a work inbox: Mindfulness for peak performance. Twelve noon, conference room B, lunch provided. Breathe, focus, reduce stress, get more done.
Nothing wrong with any of that. But one critic asks a sharper question. What if the stress is coming from something that ought to change?
A schedule nobody can meet. A boss who shouts. Then a practice that only teaches you to stay calm might be helping the problem stay put.
Today, that worry, and where mindfulness came from before it reached the conference room.

teach.h: CALM ISN'T THE SAME AS GOOD.
teach.b: First, the critique. Ronald Purser, a business professor and Buddhist teacher, wrote a book with a pointed title: McMindfulness.
He argues that mindfulness sold for productivity can be cut off from its roots, so it helps people adjust calmly to whatever is wearing them down, without asking whether that thing is right.
Calm, he says, isn't the same as good. Second, the roots.

teach.h: ONE STRAND OF AN EIGHTFOLD PATH.
teach.b: In the Buddha's first teaching, as the tradition records it, right mindfulness is one part of an eightfold path, beside right speech, right action and right livelihood: how you talk, how you act, how you earn a living.
Mindfulness there is one strand braided with the others, not a tool that floats free. Third, a line that holds the strands together.
The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind."

teach.h: NOT HARMING, DOING GOOD, THEN MIND.
teach.b: Purifying the mind comes last, after not harming and doing good. Fourth, the other side, fairly.

Defenders of secular programs say leaving the religion out lets people in hospitals and offices try a practice they'd never have tried otherwise, and that ethics can be taught without Buddhist doctrine.
Buddhist teachers themselves differ: some welcome the secular programs, some share Purser's worry.
The question is what the calm is for.

how: In Buddhist teaching, mindfulness is practiced as one part of the eightfold path alongside right speech, action and livelihood; some secular teachers also pair mindfulness practice with an ethical intention for the day.

o: a mind so calm it stops feeling anything, good or bad
mindfulness sold for calm or output, cut off from how you treat people
meditating without a teacher, a temple or any religious setting

games.q: mindfulness without ethics: tap the pairs.
p: not to commit any sin, to do good

s: in the eightfold path, mindfulness stands on its own
right mindfulness sits beside right speech, right action and right livelihood.
Purser argues calm isn't the same as good
his worry is a calm that helps people adjust to things that ought to change.
Buddhist teachers all agree with Purser's critique
they differ: some welcome secular programs, some share his worry.

games.q: you've learned to stay calm and focused at work. in a meeting, a coworker is being treated unfairly. what does mindfulness, rooted in the eightfold path, ask?
o: stay calm and keep your focus on your own work.
notice clearly, and let it shape what you say and do.
step out of the meeting to breathe.
games.why: in the eightfold path, mindfulness is braided with right speech and right action. the critics' worry is a calm that never reaches them.

practice: Before you settle, choose one small, concrete intention for today in your own words: to speak without harshness in one hard conversation, to notice who's being left out of a meeting, to tell the truth about one small thing.
Then rest with the breath, and near the end bring the intention back once and let the quiet you've gathered lean toward it. If you pray, you can offer it there.

wordCard.voice: Mindfulness without ethics. The critics' worry that a practice sold for productivity can lose the roots that tied it to how you treat people. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali, from the Buddhist texts: mindfulness, also memory or keeping in mind. Right mindfulness is sammā-sati.

carryVoice: Your line: not just calm. Calm makes good company for a good intention. Go gently.

sources.ref: Ronald Purser, McMindfulness: How Mindfulness Became the New Capitalist Spirituality
